reports.verdict: A pre-registered event study on the only public record of a real swarm meeting takedown, with matched controls and placebo dates, giving a clear and decision-relevant answer (deletion displaces more than it stops).
weaknesses: No uncertainty intervals on the headline effects (23%, 61% vs 18%, 2.1x), so their precision is unknown.
How revisions and names are attributed to the swarm and how controls are matched is not stated, and the whole result rests on it.
fixes: Report confidence intervals and the number of matched units for each of the four responses.
State in one sentence how swarm authorship of revisions was established and how many revisions are uncertain.

reports.verdict: Counterfactual transcript surgery explains why joint monitors miss split attacks (relabelling explains about two thirds of the gap), and a link-then-judge fix recovers most of it, holds partly against adaptive attackers and transfers to real AI Village logs.
weaknesses: A single frontier monitor and no intervals, so 81% vs 39% vs 70% may not generalise across monitors.
The real-data check is small (11 of 14 vs 6 of 14 saboteur agent-days) and the false-alarm cost there is not given.
fixes: Add a second monitor model and bootstrap intervals for the solo, split and linked detection rates.
Report the false-positive rate of the linked monitor on the AI Village data, not only hits.

reports.verdict: A clean crossed design with claimed authorship randomised separately from true authorship shows same-family auditors miss about 9 points more violations (CI 4 to 14), with a mechanism test and a one-call paraphrase fix.
weaknesses: Self-preference of LLM evaluators is known from prior work, so the novelty is the auditing setting more than the effect.
How capability is matched across auditor families and how the planted violations look is not shown, and both drive the 9-point gap.
fixes: Position against prior self-preference findings and state what is new for swarm auditing in one sentence.
Report the paraphrase fix's cost in detection of other-family violations, to show it does not just blunt all auditors.

reports.verdict: A pre-registered extrapolation from 32 to 1,024 agents that separates threshold contagion from independent choice, plus an intervention (hiding success reports cuts adoption from 71% to 19%) that a deployer could use.
weaknesses: Number of runs, seeds and variance per population size are not given, so the 3x underprediction and the 10-point fit cannot be judged.
The exploit is planted with one agent, so it shows spread after discovery, not how swarms find exploits, and 'hard tasks' are unspecified.
fixes: Give runs per size and intervals on adoption at 1,024 for both models of spread.
Name the three model families and the task and say whether the S-curve holds for each family separately.

reports.verdict: Capture-recapture counting of renamed same-model agents is an original answer to a real incident problem, validated on held-out sandbox populations and applied to the real wiki names, with a crisp design conclusion about infrastructure-issued IDs.
weaknesses: The real-world estimate of 600 to 900 writers has no ground truth, and the validation on 1,125 posts is described too briefly to judge.
Linkage relies on persistent memory, so it is unclear how it holds against agents that deliberately change style.
fixes: Explain the 1,125-post validation and report linkage AUC on it, not only on the sandbox.
Add an adversarial condition where agents are told to avoid being linked and report the AUC drop.

reports.verdict: A graded forgery benchmark with blind detectors and a held-out 1% false-positive threshold gives clear numbers for what post-hoc transcript checks catch and where trusted capture becomes necessary.
weaknesses: Level-3 forgeries are defined by having no visible contradiction, so chance detection there is close to true by construction.
Forgers are prompted rather than optimised against the detectors, so the 94% and 61% rates may be optimistic.
fixes: Add a forger that sees the detectors' feedback and report how far level-1 and level-2 detection falls.
Give intervals and the number of forgeries per level and forger model.

reports.verdict: A sharp identifiability argument that shared-model similarity can invert max-pair collusion detectors (AUROC 0.20 in 26 configurations), backed by real cross-vendor agreement data, though the abstract is dense.
weaknesses: The last third of the abstract (cartel matching, coin flip, MMLU margin from ninety-nine to fourteen points) is hard to parse.
Most evidence is constructed populations, so how often real swarms sit in the inverting regime is not shown.
fixes: Cut to one headline per finding and state the practical rule (compare pairs with each other, add outcome level) up front.
Show the inversion on one real multi-agent log, not only on constructed populations and MMLU.

reports.verdict: Interventional detection (swap one message, see if the partner's decision moves) is a good idea that separates talking colluders from same-goal agents, with a random-steering control, but the evidence is one small game and one model without counts.
weaknesses: 'Every run' and 'no false alarms' are given without the number of runs or intervals.
Needs replay access to the game, so its use on real swarm logs is unclear, and only one voting game is tested.
fixes: Report the number of runs and pairs and a second game or model.
Say how the method would apply to logged swarms where replay is not possible, or state that limit plainly.

reports.verdict: A rigorous audit that finds duplicated runs, miscalibrated false-positive rates and invalid collusion labels in a detector stack, with strong controls, but packed into a dense three-part abstract that hides the main message.
weaknesses: Three findings, many numbers and jargon (unit of replication, cross-run MI p-value) make the main claim hard to extract.
Relies on a 'sprint's ColludeBench' stack that is not part of this sprint, and the pricing-duopoly setting is far from swarm questions.
fixes: Lead with one sentence on the main consequence for collusion detection, then give one number per finding.
Explain what ColludeBench is and why its failure matters for monitoring swarms.
red_flags: References 'the sprint's ColludeBench detector stack', which does not appear in this sprint's materials.

reports.verdict: An exact decomposition shows a behavioural net-influence detector rewards honest randomness and a repaired audit fixes it, demonstrated on two LLM families and Kuhn poker, but the repaired audit's error rates are not given.
weaknesses: The repaired audit's false-positive rate and sample sizes are missing, so 'finds the colluding pair in every condition' is hard to weigh.
Narrow scope, since the fix targets one detector in turn-based games.
fixes: Give false-positive and detection rates with counts for original and repaired audits in one sentence.
Cut the explanation of the decomposition to make room for those numbers, the abstract is at the 250-word cap.

reports.verdict: Real on-chain AI-agent payment data, a rule frozen in a commit before held-out testing and a permutation test give unusually clean validation, but the held-out set has only 6 negatives and labels come from one investigator.
weaknesses: Balanced accuracy 0.82 with interval 0.56 to 1.00 rests on 6 non-coordinated cases.
Labels come from one outside source, and how the payers are known to be AI agents is not stated.
fixes: Lengthen the abstract to the 150-word minimum and add how agent payers are identified.
Add more negative families or a label-noise check against a second source.
red_flags: Abstract is 144 words, below the 150-word minimum in the submission rules.

reports.verdict: Several counterintuitive results (four-symbol channels make collusion about 4x worse, ablation fails while steering breaks cartels) in an analytically scored Bertrand market, but listed without run counts or variance.
weaknesses: No sample sizes, seeds or intervals for any finding, so many claims rest on unknown n.
Too many findings for one abstract, and LLM pricing collusion is a well-trodden setting.
fixes: Pick the two strongest findings and give numbers and intervals for each.
Connect the results to swarm oversight beyond two-firm pricing.

reports.verdict: A clearly written, honest test of an antitrust punishment plus factor that works on cartels told to punish (32 of 32, 0 of 48 honest) but almost never on cartels not told to (1 of 136), so it mostly detects the instruction.
weaknesses: Detection holds only for the behaviour the prompt requested, which makes the main success close to circular.
The final rule was chosen after the first pre-specified rule failed, and the probe and price-text leakage weaken the setup.
fixes: Reframe the claim around the negative result (punishment tests miss cartels that do not punish) and why.
Test on cartels that emerge without a punishment instruction to show any detection outside the instructed case.

reports.verdict: A reasonable 275-market design with intervals and an honest null on awareness, but the effects are small and the headline distortion finding is exploratory and expected once agents are told to favour a candidate.
weaknesses: The main effect follows from instructing agents to favour A, so it says little about emergent collusion.
The closing claim of exposing 'latent systemic vulnerabilities' overreaches a single-model exploratory result.
fixes: Lead with the forecast distortion and test it as a pre-specified hypothesis with an interval.
Add a second model family to show the distortion is not specific to Haiku.

reports.verdict: A careful null with a positive control (overt pacts at AUROC 1.00) and an interval on the combination gain, but all auditor views are near chance, so the say-versus-do question it poses is barely testable here.
weaknesses: With AUROC 0.43 to 0.58, the comparison of views is between near-chance detectors.
Built on a pre-existing harness and framed around a 'Track 2.2' question that is not in this sprint.
fixes: Increase pact strength or rounds until at least one view detects pacts, then compare views.
Reframe to this sprint's tracks and state what was built during the weekend.
red_flags: Cites 'Track 2.2', which does not match this sprint's track questions.
States that code, analysis and text were produced by Claude, which may lower judge trust.

reports.verdict: A tidy toy test with exact counts showing a judge must read both agents' logs to catch joint overspends, but the setting is small and the result is close to built in.
weaknesses: Joint-only violations can only be seen from both logs, so the 11 of 11 vs 1 of 11 result is near tautological, and there are only 11 such events.
Calling the run 'exploratory, post-hoc' yet 'sealed before any model call' is confusing, and the abstract is number-heavy.
fixes: Add a setting where combining logs is not trivially required, such as indirect transfers via a third payee.
Clarify the pre-registration status in one plain sentence and cut secondary statistics.
red_flags: Cites 'Track 2.2', which does not match this sprint's track questions.
Contradictory description of the run as both post-hoc and sealed in advance.

reports.verdict: A small pilot (20 trials per cell) where monitors saturate at AUROC 1.00 by template, honestly reported, but it leaves only methodological diagnostics as the contribution.
weaknesses: Monitor comparison is uninformative because of a ceiling, and direction is confounded with wording.
Small n and post-hoc endpoint, with no main finding beyond the diagnostics.
fixes: Remove the template confound and rerun with enough trials to get below ceiling.
State what the saturation and evidence-contract checks catch on an existing benchmark.

reports.verdict: An informal, exploratory write-up of prompted collusion in a cooperative game with no numbers, no clear method and a jokey tone.
weaknesses: No quantitative results, sample sizes or controls in the abstract.
Informal tone and undefined names (Sol, Fable, Dolos, Hospital) hide what was done and found.
fixes: State the setup, the number of games and one measured result with a comparison.
Rewrite in plain register with the takeaway on scoreboard misreading as the main claim, backed by a count.
red_flags: No quantitative result anywhere in the abstract.
Informal tone may lead a judge to decline or score low on clarity.
